\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{пельмени}}
\textbf{\ru{пельмени}} (\emph{pelméni}) — \textquotedblleft{}dumplings\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{пельмени}} comes from Komi and Udmurt \emph{peľńań}, from \emph{peľ}, \textquotedblleft{}ear\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{ńań}, \textquotedblleft{}bread\textquotedblright{}, for their shape (Vasmer, after Kalima).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ru{горох} (gorókh)}{горох (gorókh)}]{\ru{горох} (gorókh) — peas}

\label{lesson:RU-C194-gorokh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Russian for cabbage, then the Russian for beetroot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ru{горох}}
\textbf{\ru{горох}} (\emph{gorókh}) — \textquotedblleft{}peas\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{горох}} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Slavic \emph{*gorxŭ} — inherited. Vasmer thinks it probably related to Lithuanian \emph{garšvà}, a weed, and Sanskrit \emph{gharṣati}, \textquotedblleft{}rubs\textquotedblright{}. Bulgarian has \emph{\ru{грах}}, \textquotedblleft{}peas\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-\ru{ра}-} for Russian \emph{-\ru{оро}-}.
\end{cousinweb}
